newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador president faces hurdles on budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador president faces hurdles on budget deficit.

text.p: Ecuador's newly appointed president, who managed to emerge victorious from a political crisis, now faces the difficult task of controlling the government's budget deficit after he scrapped his predecessor's austerity measures.

The withdrawal of an economic plan put in place by ousted president Abdala Bucaram to address the fiscal gap will leave his successor, Fabian Alarcon, with a deficit of between five and seven percent of gross domestic product, analysts said.

"The worst problem will be the fiscal deficit because of the withdrawal of the economic measures -- measures that were well received and that were not opposed by the majority of people," said Diego Lavalle, an analyst at Banco Amazonas.
"The protests were against the corruption that permeated Bucaram's government," he said.
Bucaram had raised rates on electricity and gas by more than 200 percent and increased bus fares by 60 percent.

The plan, modeled on Argentina's successful Convertibility program launched in 1991, was scheduled to be introduced in the middle of this year. Argentina's former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, the author of Argentina's plan, served as an economic adviser to Bucaram.
Either way, as the Argentine experience has showed, a pegged currency system puts more contraints on fiscal policy.
"The clear problem now is fiscal. With the withdrawal of the measures, the deficit this year is likely to be around five percent of GDP," Francisco Sweet, a former finance minister, said.
"Unfortunately, all the adjustment measures lost support, although the fall of Bucaram was not because of his economic policies," he said.
A banker and official in the administration of former President Sixto Duran Ballen estimated the deficit could rise to as much as seven percent of GDP.

The banker, who did not want to be identified, said the new government would face further difficulties because it replaced Bucaram's administration amid mass social protests. The country came to a virtual standstill last week when unions staged a 48-hour general strike against Bucaram.
"This government will have to govern in a populist manner and withdraw all the measures because of the level of social agitation the country was in when it came to power," the banker said.

Among the measures Bucaram had planned was a privatization program, including the sale of 35 percent of state telephone company Emetel. The sale, in which the government hoped to raise $1.0 billion, was scheduled for April.

In addition, the government was planning to issue its first-ever Eurobonds at the beginning of this month. According to a ministry official, Chase Manhattan Bank transferred $300 million to Ecuador's central bank at the end of January as part of the credit agreement to issue the bonds.
Syndicate and emerging market debt sources on Tuesday said the issue was not likely to come to market anytime soon.
Meanwhile, because of the rise in Ecuador's rates and decline in its currency, analysts forecast 1997 inflation of more than 20 percent, exceeding the previous government's forecast.

"Inflation is not likely to be at those levels. It is very early to predict what inflation will be, but my guess would be that it could reach levels of around 36 and 38 percent," said economist Fidel Jaramillo at Gestion magazine.
Ecuador had inflation of 25 percent in 1996 and economic growth of 1.8 percent.
